name: Muircertach mac Erc

attributes.attribute: High King of Ireland in the sixth century C.E.
named for his mother Erc, a princess from Scotland
fell by the craft of Sin, who gave life to sticks and stones
the fire was an illusion; the wine took him

sources: Cross, Tom Peete, and Clark Harris Slover, eds. Ancient Irish Tales. (New York: Henry Holt and Co., 1936), 518.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Muircertach mac Erc is a king of Irish tale with a layer of history under the myth. He was the High King of Ireland in the sixth century C.E. His name holds a puzzle. It names his mother, not his father. Erc was a princess of Scotland. His father was Muirreach, a grandson of the great king Niall of the Nine Hostages. Some scholars ask if Erc was a goddess before she was a woman, but that answer does not yet explain his name. The Annals of Ulster keep a tale of his fall. He took the high kingship from the older dwellers of Tara and gave none of them quarter. Later a lovely woman named Sin offered herself to him if he would cast out his wife and children. He did, and war tore his land. The warriors who came at him were Sin's doing, dreadful though they seemed, made of sticks and stones she had given life. Muircertach had killed her kin when he took Tara. Now he broke, ran mad through the rain and snow, and came home to a vision of demons. He thought the palace was on fire and threw himself into a vat of wine. The wine drowned him. The fire was an illusion, Sin's last work.
